title: Before ≠ Because
subtitle: Two lamps, a house and a ship
learning_objective: Tell three things apart: (1) the order in which events happen; (2) empirical judgments of cause (Hume: habit of association; modern causal inference: intervention and ruling out common causes); (3) Kant’s philosophical claim that causality is a category of the understanding — a condition for experiencing an objective order in time.
disclaimer: A teaching analogy to help understand Kant — it does not prove or test his transcendental philosophy.

steps.title: Observe
steps.prompt: Watch the two lamps: A lights, then B. Watch a few rounds.

steps.title: Experiment
steps.prompt: Change the conditions and see what happens. Then look at the house and the ship.

steps.title: Judge again
steps.prompt: Do you still think A caused B?

steps.title: Explain
steps.prompt: Split what you just saw into three layers.

steps.title: Apply
steps.prompt: Check a claim from real life the same way.

steps.title: Keep
steps.prompt: Keep what you understood and what you still wonder about.

user_actions.label: Look over the house in your own order
Follow the ship in its order
Try to see the ship backwards
Write what you understood / a question

feedback_rules.say: A lights before B every time. Your mind starts to expect it: A lights, so B is coming.
You think A caused B. Keep that judgment — next you will test it.
You think not. Then why does B always follow A? Let’s find out.
Not sure is a good place to start: order alone is not enough to judge.
You pressed A yourself and B stayed dark. A always comes first, yet it is not B’s cause. This move is called intervention.
Behind the curtain a timer drives both A and B. That is a common cause (a confounder).
Stop the timer and neither lamp lights. The timer is what really does the work.
You chose the order to look at the house — roof first or door first, the house did not change. This is a subjective order.
The ship doesn’t drift backwards: you can only see it upstream first, then downstream. You don’t get to choose this order.
The ship’s order is fixed: an objective order — something really happened. Kant’s question is what entitles us to take it as objective.
You changed your mind. What changed it was not more watching, but intervening and finding the common cause.
You still think it’s cause. Remember: when you pressed A yourself, did B light?
Right: in this setup both A and B are caused by the timer. Before is not because.
You may stay unsure. But intervening already showed that A is not B’s cause.

layers.title: ① Order in time
layers.body: A happens before B. That is a fact about order; on its own it says nothing about what produces what.

layers.title: ② Empirical judgment of cause
layers.body: Hume pointed out that we never see a ‘power’ — only that B always follows A, and habit makes us expect B. Modern causal inference gives ways to test this: intervene on A yourself (not just watch), and rule out common causes (confounders) and reverse causation. That is what you just did with the lamps.
layers.source: Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739); An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding (1748); modern causal inference (intervention, randomised trials, confounding)
layers.maps_to: Press A · lift the curtain · stop the timer

layers.title: ③ Kant’s claim
layers.body: Kant held that cause and effect is one of the categories of the understanding (under Relation). It is not learned from experience; it is a condition that makes experience possible. Looking over a house, the order of your perceptions can run either way (a subjective order). Watching a ship drift downstream, the order is fixed (an objective order). Kant argues that to take a series of perceptions as an event that objectively happens, we must think it under a rule — the causal law. But the category only says every event has a cause; what causes what must still be found out from experience — layer ② again.
layers.source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (1781/1787), Second Analogy (from A189/B232; the house and ship example is in this section — check page numbers against your edition)

content.map_note: Mind the mapping: the lamps belong to layer ② (experience and method). The house and the ship are Kant’s own example for layer ③.

apply_checks.label: I only saw one thing come after the other
A third factor could cause both
It could run the other way (B causes A)

apply_verdicts.label: I think it is cause and effect
Not sure yet — need to check
